corrections.append: A fuller account, per the curator: Mary Donovan Hapgood (1886-1973) was a union organizer, a Socialist Party candidate for governor of Massachusetts, and a leading member of the Sacco-Vanzetti Defense Committee. After the executions of Sacco and Vanzetti she was arrested outside the funeral parlor where their bodies were held, on charges of advocating anarchy and inciting a riot, for carrying a placard quoting the judge who had sentenced the men: Did you see what I did to those anarchist bastards? - Judge Thayer. A year later, for speaking at a meeting of striking miners in Pittston, Pennsylvania, she was jailed four days - March 4 to March 8, 1928 - in the Luzerne County jail at Wilkes-Barre, on charges of disorderly conduct, inciting to riot, and a peace-bond proceeding, and released on bond of $2,500 individually, $5,000 combined.
corrections.case_set_charges: Disorderly conduct, inciting to riot, and a peace-bond proceeding — for speaking at a meeting of striking anthracite miners at Pittston, Pennsylvania.
corrections.case_set_sentence: Held four days, March 4-8, 1928, in the Luzerne County jail at Wilkes-Barre; released on bond of $2,500 individually ($5,000 combined with her husband Powers Hapgood).

add_case.charges: Advocating anarchy and inciting a riot — arrested outside the funeral parlor where the bodies of Sacco and Vanzetti were held, for carrying a placard quoting Judge Thayer: Did you see what I did to those anarchist bastards?
add_case.convicted: Unresolved — the arrest is documented; the disposition is not
add_case.sentence: Arrested after the August 1927 executions of Sacco and Vanzetti; jail time and disposition not documented.

corrections.note: The recorded March 1929 Pittston arrest was wrong — the curator dates the jailing March 4-8, 1928 (4 days, Luzerne County jail). Forced date corrections with old values echoed; birth/death fill empty fields; the 1927 funeral-parlor arrest enters as a second case row.

flags: powers-hapgood shares the Pittston case with the same wrong March 1929 dating and the $5,000 bail figure that the curator gives as the couple's combined bond — his record almost certainly needs the same March 4-8, 1928 correction, but the curator's note covered Mary only; left for a decision.
